accuracyBoundary: These chapters teach mechanisms and decision logic. Material-grade processing windows, machine limits, mould limits, hot-runner limits and site procedures remain controlling. Numeric examples from manufacturer documents are evidence examples only and are not universal setpoints.

chapters.title: Polymer structure: amorphous and semi-crystalline behaviour
chapters.applicability: General thermoplastic injection-moulding concepts; individual grades may behave differently because of molecular architecture, additives, reinforcement and processing history.

sections.title: Structure changes processing behaviour
sections.text: Thermoplastics do not all solidify in the same way. Amorphous materials solidify primarily as molecular mobility falls through their glass-transition region, while semi-crystalline materials can additionally form ordered crystalline regions during cooling. This distinction affects shrinkage, dimensional response, cooling behaviour and the sensitivity of properties to mould temperature and cooling history.

sections.title: Do not turn the categories into absolutes
sections.text: The labels amorphous and semi-crystalline are useful engineering starting points, not complete process specifications. Copolymers, fillers, fibres, nucleating agents, flame-retardant packages and other modifiers can materially change flow, crystallisation, shrinkage and warpage. Use the actual grade documentation and measured part behaviour when establishing a production process.

chapters.title: Viscosity, shear rate, temperature and flow behaviour
chapters.applicability: Conceptual polymer-flow guidance. Quantitative viscosity behaviour requires material-specific rheological data and the relevant temperature and shear-rate range.

sections.title: Flow resistance is not a single material number
sections.text: The apparent viscosity of a polymer melt depends on conditions. Injection moulding commonly operates in shear-dependent flow, so changing filling rate, melt temperature, geometry or material condition can change the pressure required to produce a given flow. A viscosity value without temperature, shear-rate basis and material identity is therefore incomplete.

sections.title: Pressure is evidence about the whole flow path
sections.text: Injection pressure reflects resistance through the machine nozzle, runner system, gates and cavity as well as the melt's behaviour. A pressure change does not by itself identify the cause. Troubleshooting should compare controlled conditions, process traces and physical evidence rather than assuming that a pressure symptom proves one mechanism.

chapters.title: Moisture, drying and hydrolysis without universal drying numbers
chapters.applicability: Hygroscopic and moisture-sensitive thermoplastics. Exact allowable moisture, dryer type, temperature and time are grade-specific and must come from current supplier guidance.

sections.title: Moisture can affect appearance, processing and polymer integrity
sections.text: Moisture effects depend on polymer chemistry. It can contribute to surface defects, foaming and unstable plasticising, and in hydrolysis-sensitive polymers moisture present at melt temperature can reduce molecular weight. Drying is therefore a material-control task, not merely a cosmetic adjustment.

sections.title: There is no universal drying recipe
sections.text: Supplier documents demonstrate materially different drying requirements between polymer families and grades. A time-and-temperature pair copied from another resin can be ineffective or harmful. Confirm the exact material and grade, incoming or measured moisture condition, dryer capability and current supplier requirement before setting a drying process.

sections.title: Keep the material dry after drying
sections.text: Drying performance can be lost if dried hygroscopic material is exposed to humid air during conveying, storage or machine feeding. The material path from dryer to feed throat is part of the controlled process and should be assessed when moisture-related evidence persists.

chapters.title: Residence time, thermal history and degradation
chapters.applicability: General thermoplastic processing mechanism; acceptable melt temperature and residence-time exposure are grade-specific.

sections.title: Time at temperature matters
sections.text: A polymer's thermal history is determined by more than the barrel setpoints. Melt temperature, time in the plasticising unit, delays, shot utilisation, hot-runner residence and repeated heating all contribute to exposure. Manufacturer guidance for engineering polymers explicitly treats residence time as a quality factor.

sections.title: Treat degradation as an evidence problem
sections.text: Discolouration, odour, gas, deposits, viscosity change or mechanical-property loss can be consistent with degradation, but none alone proves it. Check actual melt conditions, residence pathways, interruptions, contamination and grade-specific limits before changing the process.

chapters.title: Commodity, engineering and high-performance polymer families
chapters.applicability: Orientation only. Family names do not replace grade-level TDS, processing guides, SDS or application qualification.

sections.title: Families are useful maps, not recipes
sections.text: Polymer families help engineers anticipate broad differences in thermal behaviour, moisture sensitivity, stiffness, toughness, chemical resistance and processing demands. They are useful for asking better questions, but they do not define a production window.

sections.title: The grade is the actionable identity
sections.text: Two grades from the same polymer family may differ through molecular weight, reinforcement, flame retardants, impact modifiers, colour systems or processing aids. Production decisions should therefore resolve the full commercial grade and revision of its supplier information before relying on family-level guidance.

chapters.title: Glass fibre, mineral, flame retardants, colour and other modifiers
chapters.applicability: General modifier effects; actual property and processing consequences are formulation- and grade-specific.

sections.title: Modifiers change the material system
sections.text: Reinforcement and additives can change stiffness, flow, shrinkage, anisotropy, thermal behaviour, appearance and degradation sensitivity. Fibre orientation can make properties and shrinkage direction-dependent, which means gate location, flow pattern and part geometry can become strongly linked to warpage and dimensional behaviour.

sections.title: Do not transfer settings between modified grades by name alone
sections.text: A reinforced, flame-retarded or otherwise modified grade should be treated as its own processing material. Confirm the supplier's grade-specific processing guidance and qualification requirements rather than assuming that settings for an unfilled or differently modified resin are interchangeable.

chapters.title: Screw, barrel, non-return valve and plasticising
chapters.applicability: Reciprocating-screw injection units. Screw geometry, non-return-valve design, allowable temperatures and wear limits are machine/material specific.

sections.title: Plasticising prepares the next shot
sections.text: During screw recovery, pellets are conveyed, heated, compressed and mixed into a melt while the screw moves rearward to accumulate the next shot. Barrel heating contributes energy, but mechanical work and material behaviour also influence the resulting melt condition.

sections.title: The non-return valve matters during injection
sections.text: A check-ring or other non-return-valve system is intended to restrict reverse flow during injection so forward screw movement can displace melt toward the mould. Wear, contamination or poor sealing can contribute to shot inconsistency, but diagnosis should use repeatability evidence rather than assuming every cushion or weight variation is a valve fault.

sections.title: Hardware suitability is material dependent
sections.text: Manufacturer processing guides can specify suitable screw types, lengths, compression characteristics and nozzle arrangements for particular materials. Those requirements override generic descriptions in this Book.

chapters.title: Shot size, cushion, screw position and machine suitability
chapters.applicability: General reciprocating-screw process reasoning. Machine manufacturer limits and material residence constraints control acceptable utilisation.

sections.title: Screw position is process evidence
sections.text: The screw-position trace describes how the injection unit moves through dosing, filling, transfer and packing. Cushion is the remaining forward stroke position after the programmed injection/hold sequence, but its meaning depends on the machine's position convention and control architecture.

sections.title: Avoid universal shot-utilisation percentages
sections.text: A machine can be too large or too small for a process for several reasons, including residence exposure, plasticising capacity, available injection pressure or rate, metering repeatability and clamp requirements. A single universal percentage cannot establish suitability. Evaluate the machine, material, mould and required process window together.

chapters.title: Injection velocity, pressure and machine control
chapters.applicability: General filling-control concepts. Controller terminology, limits and transfer behaviour are machine-specific.

sections.title: Velocity command and pressure demand are different quantities
sections.text: During velocity-controlled filling, the machine attempts to move the screw according to the commanded velocity profile while pressure develops as required to overcome resistance, up to machine or programmed limits. If the available pressure is insufficient, the commanded velocity may not be achieved.

sections.title: A process should distinguish control from limits
sections.text: A pressure limit that repeatedly constrains filling is not equivalent to a deliberately pressure-controlled filling strategy. Review actual velocity, pressure and position traces to determine what the machine achieved, not only what was entered as a setpoint.

sections.title: Transfer changes the control objective
sections.text: The transition from filling to packing/holding changes what the process is trying to control. Transfer position or other transfer criteria must be interpreted with the mould filling state, machine response and process evidence. Generic transfer positions are not portable between moulds.
